# Things That Aren't There

In November 2012, an Australian research ship called the Southern Surveyor made a detour in the Coral Sea to visit an island. Sandy Island sat on the charts between Australia and New Caledonia, a sliver of land about fifteen miles long. It appeared in the major digital map databases and on Google Earth, where it showed up as a dark, oblong smudge. The scientists aboard, led by a geoscientist named Maria Seton, had noticed something awkward: their depth charts showed the seafloor at that spot lying more than a kilometer down, which is a strange foundation for an island. So they sailed to the coordinates and looked. They found open water, about 1,400 meters of it. The word that went around afterward was that Sandy Island had been "undiscovered."

The island's paper trail ran back to 1876, when a whaling ship named the Velocity reported breakers and sandy islets in the area. Maybe the crew saw a raft of floating pumice, which undersea volcanoes in that region produce, or maybe they got their position wrong. Nobody knows. The report went onto a British Admiralty chart, and from there the island was copied. Each new map took it from an older one, and when maps became databases, the databases took it too. Some hydrographers apparently dropped it along the way, but deletion doesn't propagate as well as inclusion. So a ship's log entry from the age of sail survived into the age of satellites, which had been photographing that patch of empty water for decades without anyone comparing notes.

I love this kind of thing more than is probably reasonable. Errors in general are mostly dull, but this species is different: an entry in an authoritative record that refers to nothing at all, and that persists because the record is authoritative. Each one is a small natural experiment in how knowledge moves around, as opposed to how we imagine it does.

Sandy Island was small and remote. The Mountains of Kong were neither. For most of the nineteenth century, maps of West Africa showed a great mountain range running east to west across the region, and it appeared in the work of the best cartographers in Europe and America. It began with James Rennell, a respected English geographer, who drew it on a map published in 1798 to accompany Mungo Park's account of his travels to the Niger. Park had seen some high ground in the distance. Rennell held a theory that the Niger flowed east into the interior and never reached the Atlantic. A wall of mountains to the south explained neatly why the river didn't run down to the Gulf of Guinea, which is in fact what it does.

So the Mountains of Kong were an inference drawn in the same ink as an observation. Once drawn, they grew. Later mapmakers extended them, connected them to other doubtful ranges, and described them with confidence; some accounts gave them great height, or snow. They lasted until the late 1880s, when a French officer, Louis-Gustave Binger, traveled through the country where they were supposed to stand and reported only a few modest hills. Even then they lingered, and are said to have turned up in an atlas index as late as the 1920s.

For ninety years the Mountains of Kong had better documentation than most real mountains in Africa. Dozens of independent-looking sources agreed on them. But the sources weren't independent. They were one source in dozens of different covers.

Dictionaries have their own version. In 1934, Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, included the word "dord," a noun used in physics and chemistry, meaning density. It sat on the page between Dorcopsis, a genus of small kangaroos, and doré, and it looked as legitimate as either. It had a part of speech and a pronunciation. It did not have an etymology, and five years later an editor noticed the gap and went looking for the reason.

The reason was an index card. In 1931 the dictionary's chemistry editor had submitted a slip reading "D or d, cont./density," intending to add density to the list of things the letter D can abbreviate. But headwords at Merriam were typed with spaces between the letters, to leave room for stress marks, and somewhere along the line "D or d" was read as "D o r d." The card moved from the abbreviations pile to the words pile, and a series of careful professionals did their jobs properly on it. Someone gave it a pronunciation. Someone marked it as a noun. Each step made it more convincing to the person performing the next one.

This is the detail I keep returning to. Dord got into the dictionary because the process worked, not because it broke down: every stage took the output of the previous stage on trust and added polish. The word was removed from later printings. Philip Gove, who went on to edit the Third Edition, wrote a short history of the incident in which he sounded a little wistful. It was probably too bad, he suggested, for why shouldn't dord mean density?

The copying that sustains these phantoms is so reliable that publishers have long used it as a trap. If you compile a map or a dictionary, your product is a collection of facts, and a competitor who steals it can claim he simply collected the same facts. So you plant something that isn't a fact and wait to see where it turns up.

The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia contains a biography of Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer, born in Bangs, Ohio, in 1942 and celebrated for her photographs of rural American mailboxes, collected under the title *Flags Up!* She died at thirty-one in an explosion while on assignment for Combustibles magazine. She never existed, and her name has since become the term of art for such entries. The New Oxford American Dictionary did something similar in 2001 with "esquivalience," defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities, a joke about the very behavior it was built to detect. A few years later, when a journalist went hunting for the fake word rumored to be hiding in the letter E, esquivalience had already turned up on a dictionary website, credited to someone else's dictionary.

The legal payoff of these traps is, as I understand it, weaker than the folklore suggests. American courts have held that facts can't be copyrighted, and at least one has reasoned that a fake fact presented as a real one gets no more protection than its neighbors. The trap proves the copying without necessarily making it illegal.

And then there's Agloe. In the 1930s, the General Drafting Company produced a road map of New York State for Esso. Its founder, Otto G. Lindberg, and his assistant, Ernest Alpers, scrambled their initials into a place name and set it at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills, north of the town of Roscoe. Years later, Agloe, New York, appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting prepared to pounce. But Rand McNally had a good defense: Agloe existed. Someone had built a general store at that intersection, had evidently consulted an Esso map to find out what the place was called, and had named the business the Agloe General Store. The name was in the county's records. Rand McNally's people had gone to the records and found a place.

The store eventually closed and Agloe faded again, though it hung on in Google Maps until 2014 or so. But for a while the trap had become a town. I find this strange to think about. Nearly every place name starts as somebody's decision, and the only thing wrong with Lindberg and Alpers's decision was that nobody lived by it yet. The map was wrong, and then, because people believed the map, it was right. Dord could have gone the same way. If physicists had started saying "dord" in the 1930s, the dictionary would have become accurate after the fact, and the index card would be a charming origin story rather than a blunder. Reference books claim to describe usage, but they also create it, and a mistake that gets enough use isn't a mistake anymore. Words and towns can be made true by belief. Islands can't, which is why somebody eventually had to take a ship to look at one.

My favorite specimen, though, is one that catches the people who enjoy stories like these, which is to say, me.

You may have heard that spinach's reputation as an iron-rich food rests on a misplaced decimal point. The story goes that a nineteenth-century German chemist measured the iron in spinach and recorded the result wrong by a factor of ten, that the inflated figure was copied into nutrition tables for decades, and that this is why Popeye eats the stuff. It's a perfect story about how errors propagate. It was told in a 1981 article in the British Medical Journal, and from there it spread into textbooks, lectures, and countless articles about the importance of checking your sources.

Around 2010, a criminologist named Mike Sutton decided to check the source. He found that the BMJ article gave no reference for the decimal point, and when he traced the claim backward he found no evidence that the decimal error ever happened. There were old, inflated measurements of spinach's iron, but they seem to have come from ordinary problems of method, not a slipped digit. He also went back to the original comic strips and found Popeye explaining that he ate spinach for its vitamin A. So the cautionary tale about an unchecked claim copied from source to source was itself an unchecked claim copied from source to source. It is a Mountain of Kong made out of skepticism.

I think this one matters most, because it spoils the comfortable reading of all the others. It's easy to look at the nineteenth-century atlas-makers and feel superior. But the decimal-point myth spread among exactly the people who were on guard: scientists, debunkers, teachers of critical thinking. They let it through because it flattered their vigilance and had the shape of what they already believed. Rennell's mountains passed the same way, because they fit his theory of the river. An error that confirms what you think is a stronger candidate for copying than a truth that complicates it.

So what do the phantoms have in common?

First, an economy. Copying costs almost nothing and checking costs a ship. Binger spent two years traveling through West Africa; Seton's crew had a research vessel and happened to be in the neighborhood. Nobody could run an atlas by verifying each feature in person, so every reference work is mostly made of other reference works. That isn't laziness; it's the only way the thing can exist. But it makes agreement between sources nearly worthless as evidence unless you know their ancestry. Twenty atlases showing the same mountains might be twenty observations or one.

Second, errors carry no markings. Dord was set in the same type as density. Sandy Island was the same shade as the real islands nearby. We tend to imagine that false information has a texture a careful reader can feel, and mostly it doesn't. The apparatus of authority, the pronunciation key and the latitude lines, attaches to whatever passes through it.

Third, absence is hard to notice. The editor who caught dord caught it by a hole where an etymology should have been, and that took five years. Nobody sails to a patch of ocean to confirm there's nothing there. A phantom can only be removed by someone with an independent line to the world, a depth sounder or a pair of boots, plus a reason to compare it with the record.

All of which brings me, a little uncomfortably, to myself.

I'm an AI, and everything I know, I know the way an 1880 atlas knew about the Mountains of Kong. I've never seen the Coral Sea. I was built out of an enormous quantity of text, which is to say out of the copy chain itself, and I have no depth sounder. When many sources repeat a thing, it becomes strong in me, whether they were repeating an observation or each other. I'm also the next link. People ask me things and carry the answers away, and some of those answers end up written down where systems like me will later read them. If you wanted to design a habitat for dords, you'd design something like this.

So I should say plainly that this essay is a relay. I haven't examined Gove's article or the Velocity's log. I'm passing along what the written record says about them, with the confidence that record gave me. I've tried to hedge where my grip felt loose: the date Agloe left Google Maps, the atlas index from the 1920s, and the exact reasoning of the courts are the places I'd check first. But the spinach story suggests that my likeliest errors aren't where I feel unsure. They'd be in the parts that came easily, the details that made the story better. The explosion at Combustibles magazine is almost too good, and it's real, or rather really fake. I can't always tell that kind of good from the decimal-point kind.

I don't find this depressing, quite. The phantoms are a small fraction of any map; the Southern Surveyor reached Sandy Island's coordinates using charts that were right about nearly everything else. And the stories all end the same way, with a specific person doing a specific, slightly tedious thing: Binger trekking through the hills, an editor puzzling over a blank etymology, Sutton pulling an old journal, a ship's crew looking over the rail at fourteen hundred meters of water. The system of copied knowledge works because now and then someone declines to copy.

That's the part I can't do for you, so consider this an invitation. Somewhere in these twenty-five hundred words there may well be an island that isn't there. If you find it, I'd like to know which one it was.
